question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The predictive ability of a polygenic score (PGS), measured by variance explained in an independent sample, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability. SNP-based heritability estimates capture the total additive genetic variance tagged by common variants in the discovery sample, whereas PGS construction involves finite discovery samples, imperfect LD tagging across ancestries or cohorts, and the "missing heritability" gap that arises from rare variants, structural variation, and non-additive effects not captured by standard PGS methods. Even with large N, out-of-sample prediction R² remains bounded below h²_SNP due to these partitioning and decay effects.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, because polygenic scores rely on imperfectly tagged SNPs in finite samples, so the captured variance is always bounded below total SNP heritability by linkage disequilibrium decay and incomplete tagging of causal variants.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True—LD decay and tagging limits cap PGS R² strictly below SNP h² per variance partitioning, as the score can only capture tagged variation in finite samples.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is explained by the additive effects of all SNPs in the population (i.e., the theoretical upper bound obtainable if every SNP’s true effect size were known exactly). A polygenic score, by contrast, is constructed from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, incomplete tagging, and imperfect prioritization of causal variants, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is reached only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data—an unattainable condition in practice. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by the SNPs (i.e., the variance captured by the vector of true SNP effect sizes). A polygenic score constructed with exactly those true effect sizes therefore explains precisely \(h^2_{SNP}\) in an independent sample (apart from finite-sample estimation error in the phenotype itself). Consequently the inequality “PGS \(R^2\) < \(h^2_{SNP}\)” is not strictly necessary; equality is attainable in the theoretical limit. In practice PGS \(R^2\) is lower because effect-size estimates are noisy, but the statement claims necessity, which is false.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that would be captured by an optimally weighted linear combination of the observed SNPs (i.e., using the true population effect sizes). A polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample estimates of those effect sizes. Because those estimates contain sampling error, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) (equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size). Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by an optimal linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by the SNP panel). A polygenic score is precisely such a linear combination; when its weights equal the true population effects, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) therefore equals \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the estimated weights contain error, so realized \(R^2\) falls short of the bound, but the bound itself is attainable in the infinite-data limit. Consequently the predictive ability of a PGS is not *necessarily* lower than SNP heritability; it is at most equal to it. The statement is therefore false.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_\text{SNP}\) represents the total fraction of phenotypic variance that is (in principle) capturable by the SNPs when their effects are known exactly. A polygenic score, however, is constructed from finite-sample estimates of those effects; the resulting estimation error, shrinkage, and/or imperfect tagging necessarily reduce the out-of-sample \(R^2\) below \(h^2_\text{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite training data, so the inequality is strict in any real application.

Final answer: True

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear predictor formed from all SNPs (i.e., the population-level best linear unbiased predictor). Any practical polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample GWAS estimates of the SNP effects; the resulting prediction weights therefore contain sampling error, LD mismatch, and/or shrinkage. Consequently, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the theoretical limit of infinite sample size (where the two quantities converge). The qualifier “necessarily” therefore holds for all realizable polygenic scores.

Final answer: True

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor formed from all SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on additive genetic variance tagged by the SNP panel). A polygenic score (PGS) is simply one particular linear predictor whose weights are estimated from a finite discovery sample. With infinite discovery-sample size the estimated weights converge to the population weights, so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Because arbitrarily large samples are possible in principle, the PGS \(R^2\) is not necessarily strictly lower than SNP heritability; it is bounded above by it and can approach equality asymptotically. Hence the statement is false.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by the additive effects of all measured (or imputed) SNPs in the population. A polygenic score (PGS) is a finite linear combination of estimated SNP effects; even when every SNP is included, the finite training-sample size, imperfect LD tagging, and shrinkage/selection of effect sizes ensure that the out-of-sample \(R^2\) attained by the PGS is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data would the two quantities coincide; under all realistic conditions the inequality is therefore strict. Hence the statement is true.

(The answer is independent of any particular PGS construction method—PRS-CS, LDpred, SBayesR, etc.—because all are subject to the same statistical limits.)
